name: Elena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, on site by quarter to seven, because I like to walk the deck before the lads arrive. I run the formwork crew for a contractor that builds social housing, mostly five and six storey blocks for the housing association. We build the timber and ply moulds that the concrete gets poured into, so if my shuttering is out by ten millimetres, the whole floor above is out by ten millimetres. I'm also the union rep on site, which means half my lunch break goes on somebody's overtime sheet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a pour day. Everyone's tense, the pump's roaring, and then you strike the forms a few days later and there's a clean slab that'll stand for a hundred years, and people will raise kids in it. What wears me out is the paperwork that's crept in, and my knees, honestly. I'm fifty-eight, I've got two grown-up kids and a husband, Marc, who drives the number 14 bus, and I've told him I'll hang up the belt at sixty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Before we start, have you used any of the AI tools people talk about, like the chat programs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. My daughter Sophie put one on my phone and I deleted it the same night. I don't need a machine to tell me how to brace a column, and I don't like the idea of it listening to me. I'm not proud of being stubborn, but I'm not ashamed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. At the site meeting I'd say, right, can we stop talking about robots and start talking about the scaffold ties on block C. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union saying the real issue was always pay and safety, not gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get my last four years the way I planned them. I finish the Holloway Road job, maybe one more block, then I retire with the union pension and our savings and the flat paid off. It's a relief, if I'm honest, because I never wanted to learn a whole new way of working at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes for me, really. I keep running the crew, keep training the two apprentices, Kofi and Jess, and keep the same retirement date. If the office starts using some AI for the schedules, I'd let the site manager deal with it and keep my clipboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the ground stays where it is. A bit smug, maybe, but mostly just steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the paperwork that's crept in. Would a bit of time saved there matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it really took the forms off me, sure, but I've heard that one before. When they brought in the tablet for the safety checks, it took me twice as long for a year. So I'd believe it when I see my evenings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess, mostly. She's twenty, first woman apprentice I've had in years, and she's been worried she's training for a trade that won't exist. In this picture I'd tell her to stop reading the news and learn to read a drawing properly, because that's still the job.

S0.say: I'd tell the site meeting to stop talking about robots and get back to the scaffold ties. I'd share a union post saying pay and safety were always the real issue.
S0.think: It means I get my last four years as planned and retire at sixty-two on the union pension and our savings. It's a relief, because I never wanted to learn a whole new way of working.
S0.do: Keeps running the formwork crew and training her two apprentices with no change to her retirement date. Leaves any office AI to the site manager and sticks with her clipboard.
S0.feel: Calm and steady, with a touch of smugness.
S0.quote: In this picture I'd tell her to stop reading the news and learn to read a drawing properly, because that's still the job.
S0.fieldNote: Elena treats this as vindication of her refusal to touch AI tools. Her first thought went to her apprentice Jess rather than herself, which suggests the union-rep role shapes how she sees every change. She's sceptical of time-saving promises because of a bad experience with the safety tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in writing. Any new kit on site, any change to how we work, it goes through the safety committee and the union first. Online I'd probably share the union's line on retraining money, because if the jobs are shifting, the companies making money from it should pay for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me personally, not that much. Formwork on a real site, in the rain, with every block a bit different, isn't something they'll get a robot to do in a few years. But the drawing office will shrink, and the estimators, and I'd worry the firm uses it as an excuse to cut corners and squeeze the crews harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a proper agreement on the site, something that says no one loses hours because of new kit without a consultation. I'd go to the regional union meetings again, which I stopped doing two years ago. And I'd make sure Kofi and Jess got whatever training was going, even if I didn't take it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not for me so much, but for the people coming up behind me. It feels like watching weather come in from a distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make sure the apprentices got training but not take it yourself. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they've got forty years ahead and I've got four. It's not worth me sitting in a classroom learning some software when I'll be gone before it pays off. That's not me being lazy, it's arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big contractors and the developers, every time. They'd use it to cut the wage bill and keep the savings, not build more homes. Government should be making them share it, the way they should've made them share it with every other change.

S1.say: Any new kit or change to how we work has to go through the safety committee and the union first. The companies making money from AI should pay for retraining.
S1.think: Her own formwork work is too varied and outdoor for robots in a few years. She worries the firm will use AI as an excuse to cut corners and squeeze crews, and that the drawing office will shrink.
S1.do: Pushes for a site agreement that no one loses hours to new kit without consultation, and starts going back to regional union meetings. Makes sure her apprentices get training while skipping it herself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of the younger workers behind her.
S1.quote: They've got forty years ahead and I've got four. It's not worth me sitting in a classroom learning some software when I'll be gone before it pays off.
S1.fieldNote: Her response to change is organising, not adapting. She sees her own job as safe and frames refusal to retrain as arithmetic rather than fear. Blame lands squarely on contractors and developers, with government cast as the one who should force sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a big jump from the last. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at every meeting: slow it down. You can't let something like that loose on a building site with no rules, people will get killed. Online I'd be signing every petition going, and I'd probably be on the march too, knees or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm sixty when it lands. I'd be all right, really, we've got the savings and the flat, and the pension. But my son Luca works in a parcel warehouse, and that's the first place the robots go, so it's his life I'd be lying awake over, and the whole crew's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Marc and talk about me stopping at sixty instead of sixty-two, maybe sooner, rather than being pushed. I'd put everything I have into the union fight, because the first year is when the deals get made. And I'd tell Luca he can move back into his old room if it comes to that, rent free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we're covered, but tight in the chest. Mostly it feels like everything happens before anyone's had a chance to vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you choose, stay and fight, or retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, which I know sounds daft. I'd retire from the tools but not from the union, I'd keep going to the meetings as a retired member. You don't stop being a rep just because you've stopped pouring concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with Luca actually sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring him on a Sunday, because he's never up before noon on his day off. I'd say, love, your room's still there and your dad's still got the van, nobody's sinking. Then I'd probably hang up and cry in the kitchen where Marc can't see.

S2.say: Slow it down, because letting it loose on building sites with no rules will get people killed. She'd sign every petition and join the march.
S2.think: At sixty she'd be covered by savings, the paid-off flat and the pension. What keeps her awake is her son's warehouse job and her crew.
S2.do: Talks with her husband about retiring at sixty or sooner instead of sixty-two, before she's pushed. Throws herself into the union fight in the first year and offers her son his old room rent free.
S2.feel: Anxious and tight in the chest, but not panicked because the family is covered.
S2.quote: I'd say, love, your room's still there and your dad's still got the van, nobody's sinking. Then I'd probably hang up and cry in the kitchen where Marc can't see.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year speed pushes her from organising for others to fearing for her own son. She is financially safe and knows it, so her anxiety is about family and fairness rather than money. Her plan to keep being a rep after retiring shows how much of her identity sits in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like the last one, but with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse, get the rules written now, get a fund set up for people who lose their work. I'd say it in the canteen and I'd say it to our local councillor, who I've known since school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, so I'd have retired already on my own timetable. That's a strange thought, that I'd just slip out before it hits. What I'd really think about is Jess, because she'd be just out of her apprenticeship with nothing to step into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-two like I planned, no rush. I'd spend the years pushing the union to bargain for a transition deal, things like retraining paid at full wage and early pensions for the older ones. And I'd put a bit more aside each month for the kids, a few hundred, in case either of them needs help with a deposit or a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel lucky, which makes me feel a bit guilty. It's like getting off a train one stop before it crashes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never learn the new tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that might sound pig-headed, but I'd rather put those five years into the people. Let Jess learn the robots, I'll make sure she gets paid fairly for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jess, if she asked whether to finish her apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish it. A trade teaches you how a building actually stands up, and nobody can take that out of your head. But I'd also tell her to get her name on whatever course the firm offers for the machines, the very first week.

S3.say: Five years means there's no excuse: write the rules now and set up a fund for people who lose their work. She'd say it in the canteen and to her local councillor.
S3.think: She'd have retired at sixty-three before it hits, which feels strange. Her real worry is her apprentice Jess finishing her training with nothing to step into.
S3.do: Keeps her planned retirement date and spends the years pushing the union for a transition deal with paid retraining and early pensions. Puts a few hundred a month aside to help her children with a deposit or a gap.
S3.feel: Uneasy and lucky, with some guilt about getting out just before it hits.
S3.quote: I feel lucky, which makes me feel a bit guilty. It's like getting off a train one stop before it crashes.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change her refusal to learn the tools; it just gives her more time to organise. She is visibly relieved to be retired before the end point, and that relief comes with guilt. Her advice to Jess is practical and splits the difference between trade pride and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so if it goes wrong it's because someone chose for it to go wrong. I'd be saying that at the retired members' branch, because I'd be one by then, and probably in letters to the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's almost nothing. I'll be sixty-eight, retired six years, probably doing the garden and minding grandchildren. It's my kids and their kids who'd be in it, and the question is whether the money from all that work goes to everyone or to a few people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change my plans at all. I'd retire at sixty-two, keep my union card, and campaign for things like a shorter working week and a proper share of the gains. I'd probably help Sophie and Luca think about which way to jump while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Like a tax bill you know is coming but isn't due yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about fairness a lot. What does fair look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair is the robot pours the slab and the person who used to pour it still gets a decent life. If the machine does the work, the work's still been done, so somebody's getting paid for it. That money should come back round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if you imagined a building site full of robots in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The noise, funnily enough, the radio and the shouting. And the tea at ten. I can't picture a robot crew stopping for a brew and arguing about football, and I think something goes missing when nobody does.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly, so if it goes wrong someone chose that. She'd say it at the retired members' branch and in letters to the paper.
S4.think: She'll be sixty-eight and long retired, so it barely touches her. What matters is whether the gains from all that work go to everyone or just a few.
S4.do: Keeps her retirement plan unchanged and stays in the union as a retired member. Campaigns for a shorter working week and a share of the gains, and helps her children decide which way to jump.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a bill that isn't due yet.
S4.quote: I can't picture a robot crew stopping for a brew and arguing about football, and I think something goes missing when nobody does.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Elena's personal stake nearly disappears and the conversation becomes about fairness and what a site feels like. Her definition of fair is concrete and unchanged across scenarios. The loss she names isn't money but the tea break and the talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's the one where nobody gets a say, and my son's in the firing line. What would help is the government stepping in quickly with proper income support for people like Luca, and a law that says firms consult the workers before they bring robots on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. It took me thirty years to get a crew that wasn't all men, and I'd hate to see that undone because the first people let go are the newest ones. Last in, first out always hits the people who only just got through the door.

headlineQuote: Last in, first out always hits the people who only just got through the door.
portrait: Elena Moreau is a 58-year-old formwork foreperson on social housing blocks and the union rep on her site, four years from a planned retirement she has already promised her husband. She has never used an AI tool and doesn't intend to, and she frames that refusal as arithmetic rather than fear. In every scenario her instinct is to organise for others: her apprentices, her crew and her son, who works in a parcel warehouse. Fast AGI makes her anxious for family, not money, and she'd retire early but keep fighting as a retired member. The slower pictures leave her uneasy and a little guilty that she'll be out before it hits.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because nobody gets a say and her son's warehouse job is in the firing line.
whatWouldHelp: Quick government income support for people like her son, and a law requiring firms to consult workers before bringing robots on site.
